stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because almond flowers must be cross-pollinated, growers in California have long rented honeybee hives at high densities, reasoning that more hives in an orchard translate directly into more nuts. A 2025 survey of forty orchards by agronomist Lucía Ferrer complicates that reasoning. Orchards bordered by wildflower hedgerows hosted abundant wild bees, and in those orchards yields were statistically indistinguishable whether growers stocked two hives per acre or the customary five. These results cast doubt on the assumption that ______
choices: wild bees pollinate almond flowers more efficiently than honeybees do.
an orchard's almond yield rises in step with the number of hives it holds.
almond flowers can set nuts without being cross-pollinated by any bee.
growers can safely cut hive numbers in every California almond orchard.
explanation: The old view comes before the contrast: growers assumed that more hives directly produce more nuts. Ferrer's survey attacks exactly that reasoning, because in hedgerow orchards, going from five hives per acre down to two made no measurable difference to yield. The blank needs the old idea being doubted, so the answer is the one that restates it: yield rises in step with the number of hives.

A.why: You picked a new claim on the study's side of the contrast, and a stronger one than the study tested. The survey compared hive densities. It never measured how efficiently wild bees pollinate compared with honeybees. Similar yields don't show that one kind of bee works better, and a new claim isn't the old idea the blank asks for.

C.why: The passage opens by saying almond flowers must be cross-pollinated. Nothing in the survey challenges that, since the orchards still had honeybees and many wild bees. This choice reverses a fact the passage states.

D.why: This is strength creep. The finding applies only to orchards bordered by hedgerows that had plenty of wild bees. 'Every California almond orchard' stretches it to orchards the result doesn't cover. It also gives practical advice rather than naming the assumption being doubted.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some astronomers have interpreted the irregular dimming of a star cataloged as KS-219 as the work of a swarm of comets crossing in front of it. Comets shed fine dust, and fine dust blocks blue light more strongly than red light, so dips caused by comets should be deepest at blue wavelengths. However, when Ayumi Tanaka's team observed several dips at multiple wavelengths at once, each dip was equally deep in blue and red light (a pattern consistent with far larger objects), casting doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the star's dips in brightness are caused by comets passing in front of it.
the star's dips in brightness are caused by large planetesimals orbiting it.
fine dust blocks red light more strongly than it blocks blue light.
any orbiting material passes close enough to the star to dim it.
explanation: The old view is that comets cause the dimming, and it rests on a prediction: comet dust should make the dips deepest in blue light. Tanaka's team found the dips equally deep in blue and red light, which undercuts that exact prediction. What's being doubted is the old view, so the answer restates it: the dips are caused by passing comets.

B.why: You landed on the wrong side of 'however.' Larger objects are what the new evidence points toward, so they aren't what's being doubted. This choice also goes further than the text, because the passage says only that the pattern is 'consistent with' larger objects and never names planetesimals or confirms that they're there.

C.why: The passage says fine dust blocks blue light more strongly than red light. This choice reverses that relationship. The new observations don't question how dust affects light. They question whether comet dust is the cause of the dimming.

D.why: The observations don't show that nothing is dimming the star. They suggest far larger objects may be doing it. Doubting that any material dims the star claims much more than the evidence supports, and it goes against the passage's own suggestion of larger bodies.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Historians long assumed that the elaborate cadenzas in the published violin concertos of Aurelia Fontane (1741–1803) were supplied by her Paris publisher, since none of her surviving autograph scores includes a cadenza. However, a recently catalogued set of Fontane's own rehearsal parts contains cadenzas in her handwriting that match the printed versions note for note. This discovery casts doubt on the idea that ______
choices: Fontane herself wrote the cadenzas that appear in her published concertos.
the cadenzas in Fontane's published concertos originated with her publisher.
Fontane composed cadenzas for every concerto she performed in public.
Fontane's rehearsal parts were prepared after her concertos were printed.
explanation: Start by finding the old view: historians thought the publisher supplied the cadenzas, because Fontane's autograph scores have none. The new evidence is cadenzas in Fontane's handwriting that match the printed ones note for note. That attacks the publisher theory directly. The blank follows 'casts doubt on the idea that,' so it has to restate the old view. That is choice B.

A.why: This is what the new evidence supports, not what it doubts. You attached the choice to the wrong side of 'However.' The discovery points toward Fontane writing the cadenzas, so it can't cast doubt on that idea.

C.why: The rehearsal parts cover the cadenzas in her published concertos. They say nothing about every concerto she ever performed. You stretched a specific finding into an 'every' claim that the passage never tests.

D.why: The passage never says when the rehearsal parts were made, and the old view wasn't about their date. You picked a side detail instead of the claim the discovery actually challenges.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Engineers long assumed that the fine cracks found in the ceramic coatings of turbine blades were produced by thermal cycling, the repeated heating and cooling of an engine as it starts and stops, because the cracks were most common on blades from engines that cycled often. However, in a recent laboratory test, coatings held at a constant high temperature developed the same cracks when exposed to humid air, while identical coatings kept in dry air did not crack. These results challenge the assumption that ______
choices: humid air can contribute to the cracking of the ceramic coatings.
the coatings would never crack in dry air under any conditions.
the cracks were most common on blades from frequently cycled engines.
the cracks cannot form unless a coating is repeatedly heated and cooled.
explanation: The old view says thermal cycling produces the cracks. The test held the coatings at a constant temperature, so there was no cycling, and the same cracks still formed in humid air. That shows cycling isn't required for cracking. Choice D restates the old assumption, which is what the results challenge.

A.why: This is what the new test supports. You picked a claim from after 'However' when the blank needs the view the test argues against.

B.why: Look at 'never' and 'under any conditions.' The dry-air samples were tested at one constant temperature only. Also, nobody held this view before the test, so it can't be the assumption being challenged.

C.why: This is the observation the old view was based on, and the new test doesn't dispute it. The test attacks the conclusion drawn from that observation, not the observation itself.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some city officials have credited a new school nurse program with the drop in childhood asthma hospitalizations that began in 2015, the year the program launched. However, a regional analysis found that hospitalizations fell by a similar margin in nearby towns that never adopted the program, and that the decline in every community coincided with the closure of an upwind coal-fired power plant. These findings call into question the claim that ______
choices: the nurse program was chiefly responsible for the city's falling hospitalizations.
the plant closure coincided with falling hospitalizations across the region.
school nurse programs fail to improve children's health in any community.
the nearby towns had fewer asthma hospitalizations than the city before 2015.
explanation: The officials' view is that the nurse program caused the drop. They based this on timing: the decline started the year the program launched. The analysis found the same drop in towns that never had the program, so the timing no longer points to the program. Choice A restates the officials' claim, which is what the findings call into question.

B.why: This is something the analysis establishes, so it can't be what the analysis questions. You put the choice on the wrong side of 'However.'

C.why: Look at 'fail' and 'any community.' The analysis only raises doubt about whether this one program caused this one decline. It doesn't show that such programs never help anywhere.

D.why: The passage compares how much hospitalizations fell, not the towns' rates before 2015. You chose a detail the passage doesn't address and that has nothing to do with the officials' claim.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seismologists have long interpreted swarms of small earthquakes beneath Mount Kerrigan as a sign that magma was rising toward the surface, since comparable swarms preceded eruptions at other volcanoes. But a new analysis shows that the swarm quakes originated along a fault several kilometers east of the volcano's magma chamber and grew more frequent each spring, when snowmelt raises groundwater pressure. This analysis casts doubt on the idea that ______
choices: snowmelt alone triggers every earthquake that occurs beneath Mount Kerrigan.
rising groundwater pressure may influence when the swarms tend to occur.
the swarms indicate that magma is moving upward beneath the volcano.
comparable swarms have come before eruptions at other volcanoes.
explanation: The old view reads the swarms as a sign of rising magma. The new analysis places the quakes on a fault away from the magma chamber and links their timing to spring snowmelt. Both findings undercut the magma explanation. Choice C restates that old interpretation, which is what the analysis casts doubt on.

A.why: Look at 'alone' and 'every.' The passage says the swarms grew more frequent in spring. It doesn't say snowmelt is the only trigger for every quake under the volcano.

B.why: This is what the new analysis suggests, not what it doubts. You attached the choice to the wrong side of 'But.'

D.why: This is the evidence the old view relied on, and the new analysis doesn't dispute it. The analysis challenges what those swarms were taken to mean at Mount Kerrigan, not the record at other volcanoes.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many engineers have attributed the longevity of the stone arch bridges built by the Harlow & Pike company in the 1800s to their unusually thick piers. However, a survey of 40 of the firm's bridges found that those with slender piers have remained in service just as long as those with thick ones. Nearly all of the surviving bridges, it turned out, had been laid with mortar containing crushed brick. The survey thus challenges the view that ______
choices: mortar containing crushed brick may help explain the bridges' durability.
thick piers account for how long the firm's bridges have lasted.
thick piers offer no structural benefit to any kind of bridge.
the firm built more bridges with slender piers than with thick ones.
explanation: The engineers' view is that thick piers explain why the bridges lasted so long. The survey found that bridges with slender piers lasted just as long, which undercuts that explanation. Choice B restates the engineers' view, which is what the survey challenges.

A.why: This is the idea the survey points toward, not the one it challenges. You picked the new explanation from after 'However' instead of the old view being overturned.

C.why: Look at 'no benefit' and 'any kind of bridge.' The survey covered 40 bridges built by one firm. Applying it to every bridge goes far beyond that sample.

D.why: The passage never says how many bridges of each type the firm built. You chose a claim the passage doesn't address and that isn't the view the survey challenges.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: For decades, highway engineers attributed the surface cracking on concrete bridge decks mainly to heavy truck traffic, pointing out that cracking was most widespread on the busiest interstate bridges. However, a 2024 survey by civil engineer Tomás Ibarra found that decks on lightly used rural bridges built with the same concrete mix cracked at nearly identical rates. Ibarra's findings therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the concrete mix used in these decks makes them prone to cracking.
heavy truck traffic is the principal cause of cracking in these decks.
rural bridges develop cracks faster than busy interstate bridges do.
cracking on bridge decks has become more widespread in recent decades.
explanation: The old view was that truck traffic causes the cracking, and its evidence was that busy bridges cracked most. Ibarra found that bridges with little traffic cracked at nearly the same rate, which attacks that exact reasoning. If traffic were the main cause, the quiet bridges should have cracked much less. The view being doubted is the one about truck traffic.

A.why: You chose a possible new explanation, which sits on the wrong side of the 'however.' The shared concrete mix points toward this idea, but the survey never tested it. Either way, the blank asks for the old view being doubted, not a new one being suggested.

C.why: You turned 'nearly identical rates' into a difference. The passage says the two kinds of bridges cracked about equally, not that rural bridges cracked faster.

D.why: You picked a claim the passage never brings up. The survey compares busy and quiet bridges. It says nothing about whether cracking has increased over time, so it can't cast doubt on that.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Historians have long assumed that the empty interiors on seventeenth-century printed maps of the Gold Coast reflected how little European mapmakers knew about the land beyond the shore. But in workshop correspondence, archivist Hana Kostova found that several of these mapmakers owned detailed travelers' accounts of inland river routes and towns, none of which appeared on their published maps. Kostova's discovery casts doubt on the idea that the blank interiors ______
choices: were left empty to keep valuable trade routes secret from rivals.
were based on information gathered from travelers' inland accounts.
resulted from mapmakers having no information about the interior.
made the printed maps less useful to merchants traveling inland.
explanation: The old assumption was that the interiors were blank because mapmakers didn't know what was there. Kostova shows that some mapmakers did have inland information and still left it off the maps. That directly undercuts the lack-of-knowledge explanation, so this is the idea being doubted.

A.why: You added a motive the passage never gives. Kostova shows that the mapmakers left out information they had, but nothing explains why. Secrecy might be one reason, but the passage doesn't establish it. It's also a new idea, not the old view being doubted.

B.why: You reversed the finding. The travelers' accounts 'never appeared' on the published maps, so the blank interiors weren't drawn from them. Nobody held this view in the first place, so the discovery can't cast doubt on it.

D.why: You chose a point about how useful the maps were, which the passage never discusses. Kostova's evidence concerns why the interiors were blank, not how merchants used the maps.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Some ornithologists interpret the dawn singing of male Carolina wrens as aimed mainly at rival males, because singing peaks in early spring, when neighboring males are competing for territory. In a three-year study, however, Adaeze Okafor found that males sang just as often at dawn after territorial boundaries had settled, and that their singing declined sharply only once their mates began incubating eggs. These results cast doubt on the claim that ______
choices: a male wren's dawn song is directed chiefly at attracting a mate.
a male wren's dawn singing declines once incubation is underway.
a male wren's dawn song is directed chiefly at deterring rivals.
a male wren stops defending his territory once boundaries settle.
explanation: The earlier interpretation was that dawn song targets rival males, based on singing peaking during territorial competition. Okafor found that singing stayed high after the competition ended and dropped only when nesting began. That undercuts the reasoning behind the rival-male view, so it is the claim being doubted.

A.why: You picked the idea the new evidence points toward, which is the wrong side of the 'however.' The link to incubation hints that song may concern mates, but the study doesn't establish that it is 'chiefly' for attracting one. Either way, the blank needs the view being doubted.

B.why: You chose one of Okafor's own findings. The passage says singing 'declined sharply' once incubation began, so the study supports this claim rather than doubting it.

D.why: You inferred something the passage never says. Okafor measured singing, not territorial defense, so the study gives no basis for saying males stop defending their territories. It's also a different claim from the one being questioned.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Seismologists have long reported that faults within 10 kilometers of large reservoirs record roughly three times as many small earthquakes per year as comparable faults farther away. Many have attributed this gap to the weight of stored water stressing the rock below. However, nearly all of the seismometers in those surveys stood close to dams. When geophysicist Lucía Ferrante's team installed equally dense networks along both groups of faults, the two groups recorded nearly identical yearly counts, casting doubt on the idea that ______
choices: faults near reservoirs actually experience fewer small earthquakes each year than distant faults do.
dense seismometer networks detect more small earthquakes than sparse networks placed along similar faults.
stored reservoir water causes nearby faults to produce more small earthquakes than distant faults produce.
the weight of stored water determines the size of the largest earthquakes along nearby faults.
explanation: The old view says reservoir water makes nearby faults produce more small earthquakes. That view rested on a threefold gap in counts. Ferrante's team gave both groups of faults equally dense networks, and the gap disappeared. So the evidence the old view relied on now looks like a result of where the instruments were placed. The doubted idea is the old explanation, and this choice restates it.

A.why: The new study found nearly identical counts, not a reversal. You turned 'no gap' into 'the gap runs the other way', which is a stronger claim than the data support.

B.why: This is what the new evidence points toward, so it isn't being doubted. You picked an idea from the wrong side of the 'however'. The blank asks for the old view that the study undercuts.

D.why: Both the surveys and the new study counted small earthquakes. Neither measured how large the biggest earthquakes were, so the study can't cast doubt on a claim about earthquake size.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: At several Bronze Age sites, storage pits in hilltop villages held about four times as much charred barley as pits in nearby valley villages. Archaeologists long took this as evidence that hilltop communities farmed barley far more intensively than their valley neighbors. Recently, however, Mira Halvorsen analyzed chemical signatures in the hilltop grains and found that most of them matched the soils of the valley floor, not the thin soils of the hills, casting doubt on the claim that ______
choices: hilltop communities grew more barley in their own fields than valley communities grew.
hilltop villages kept more barley in their storage pits than valley villages kept.
valley farmers regularly traded their barley to hilltop villages in exchange for goods.
barley was the only grain that people in the hilltop villages relied on for food.
explanation: The old claim is that hilltop communities farmed more barley. The evidence for it was the larger stores in hilltop pits. Halvorsen found that most of the hilltop grain grew in valley soil, so a large store no longer shows large hilltop harvests. That puts in doubt the old interpretation about who grew the barley, which this choice restates.

B.why: The fourfold difference in storage is a measured finding, and the new study doesn't challenge it. You confused the evidence the old view rested on with the old view itself. The amount stored isn't in doubt. What's in doubt is what that amount was taken to show.

C.why: This sits on the new-evidence side of the 'however', and it adds a step the study never tested. Grain grown in valley soil could have reached the hills in several ways. The passage doesn't establish trade, and it isn't the idea being doubted.

D.why: Neither the old view nor the new analysis deals with other grains. You took a choice that mentions the right topic but not the claim the evidence undercuts.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: In many songbird species, city birds sing about 300 hertz higher than rural birds of the same species. Some researchers interpret this gap as birds adjusting their pitch from moment to moment to rise above the low rumble of the traffic around them. But when a two-month road closure cut traffic noise in one city by half, ornithologist Kwame Asante found that the gap between that city's birds and nearby rural birds stayed the same, casting doubt on the idea that ______
choices: city birds of these species sing at a higher pitch than rural birds of the same species do.
the difference in pitch between city and rural birds is inherited rather than learned over time.
traffic noise in the city fell by about half during the two months the roads were closed.
city birds raise their pitch in direct response to the level of traffic noise around them.
explanation: The interpretation being challenged says city birds raise their pitch in response to the traffic noise around them at the time. If so, cutting the noise in half should have narrowed the 300-hertz gap. It didn't change at all. That undercuts the moment-to-moment explanation, and this choice restates it.

A.why: The pitch gap is the observed fact, and Asante's study confirms it still holds. You chose the observation that the old interpretation explains, not the interpretation that the new evidence doubts.

B.why: This is a possible alternative explanation, not the idea under doubt, and the study never tested inheritance. The steady gap is consistent with inheritance, but it is equally consistent with learning that took place earlier in a bird's life. You landed on the new-evidence side of the 'but' and made a claim stronger than the data support.

C.why: This is a background detail of the experiment, and the passage presents it as true. It doesn't name any view that the result calls into question.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because their walls are nearly three meters thick, the hilltop enclosures of the Varda Plateau have long been described as forts. A recent excavation, however, found that the walls are made of loose rubble with no mortar, a construction that would have collapsed quickly under assault, and that each enclosure has a single entrance more than four meters wide. Large deposits of animal bone near the entrances suggest the sites may instead have hosted seasonal gatherings. These findings cast doubt on the idea that ______
choices: the enclosures may have been used for gatherings held at certain seasons.
the walls of the enclosures were thinner than earlier surveys had reported.
the enclosures were designed mainly to defend their occupants from attack.
the builders of the enclosures were unable to make or use any mortar.
explanation: The old view, from before the 'however', is that the enclosures were forts, and it rested on how thick the walls were. The new evidence goes after exactly that reasoning: rubble walls that would collapse under assault and a very wide entrance make no sense for a defensive building. The thing being doubted is the old view, that the enclosures were built mainly for defense.

A.why: The passage does support this, but it sits on the wrong side of the 'however'. It's the new possibility the bone deposits point to, not the old idea the evidence casts doubt on. You picked a true statement instead of the view being overturned.

B.why: The passage never questions the thickness of the walls. It accepts that they are nearly three meters thick and questions only what that thickness was taken to mean. This choice turns the evidence around.

D.why: The excavation shows only that these walls were built without mortar. It says nothing about whether the builders could use mortar at all. To get here you had to add an assumption the passage doesn't contain.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Astronomers have long reasoned that an asteroid rotating once every two hours or faster must be a single solid rock, since a loose pile of rubble spinning that quickly would fly apart. However, measurements of the asteroid Ilvana, which completes a rotation every 90 minutes, indicate a density so low that its interior likely contains large empty gaps, a hallmark of rubble piles. The finding challenges the assumption that ______
choices: the interior of Ilvana contains a considerable amount of empty space.
rapidly rotating asteroids are necessarily composed of one solid body.
Ilvana rotates more slowly than the speed astronomers considered critical.
most asteroids in the solar system are loosely bound piles of rubble.
explanation: Before the 'however', astronomers held that any asteroid spinning once every two hours or faster must be solid. Ilvana spins faster than that and still looks like a rubble pile, which hits the reasoning directly. What gets challenged is the old rule: that fast-spinning asteroids must be single solid bodies.

A.why: This is what the new measurements suggest, so it sits on the new-evidence side of the 'however'. The blank asks for the assumption being challenged, not for the finding that challenges it.

C.why: Ilvana turns once every 90 minutes, which is faster than the two-hour threshold, not slower. This choice reverses a number the passage states.

D.why: The passage covers one asteroid and hedges even that with 'likely'. Nobody tested a claim about most asteroids. You went from a single case to the whole solar system.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Because antibody levels in the blood of people who recover from Kessel virus drop sharply within a year, researchers have generally concluded that immunity to the virus is short-lived. A new study, however, found that memory T cells residing in lung tissue persisted for at least five years after infection and multiplied rapidly when exposed to the virus in the laboratory. These results cast doubt on the view that ______
choices: memory T cells can survive in lung tissue for years after an infection.
antibody levels in the blood stay elevated for at least five years.
lung-resident T cells by themselves prevent every case of reinfection.
protection against Kessel virus fades within roughly a year of recovery.
explanation: The old view is that immunity is short-lived, and it rested on blood antibodies falling within a year. The study finds a second line of defense, lung T cells that last five years and still respond, so falling antibodies may not mean protection is gone. The view being doubted is that protection fades within about a year.

A.why: The study supports this directly, so it belongs on the new-evidence side of the 'however'. You picked a true finding when the blank wants the old view it undercuts.

B.why: The passage says blood antibody levels drop sharply within a year. It's the T cells, not the antibodies, that last five years. This choice gives one finding to the wrong part of the immune system.

C.why: The study shows the T cells last and respond in the laboratory. It never tests whether they alone stop reinfection in people, let alone in every case. Watch for 'every' and 'by themselves': this is strength creep.
